title: Fortune's wheel
hook: Lady Philosophy: Fortune turns her wheel, and you knew she was fickle (Consolation 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Theodoric, the king Boethius served before his fall. Your line was philosophy visits: a wise visitor in a prison cell.

Your team wins the championship one year and finishes last the next. A stock soars, then sinks. A friend's business is on the news in spring and closed by fall. Up, then down, and the down tends to land as something personal. Medieval artists drew it as a great wheel: a crowned figure at the top, someone falling off the side, someone crushed at the bottom. One book gave that wheel a voice, the book from yesterday. Today: Fortune's wheel.
screen: `CHAMPIONS ONE YEAR, LAST THE NEXT.` → `A WHEEL, A CROWN, A FALL.` → `FORTUNE'S WHEEL.`

segments.voice: First, the diagnosis. In book two of the Consolation, Philosophy tells Boethius he isn't suffering because Fortune changed. He's suffering because he forgot what she is. You knew her, she says. Her only constancy is change. If she stopped turning, she wouldn't be Fortune. Second, Fortune speaks. Philosophy lets her talk for herself, and Fortune says, in effect: everything you had, wealth, honors, family glory, was mine, lent to you. I turn my wheel; that's my game. I bring the low up and the high down. Climb on if you like, but don't call it unjust when the turn brings you down. Third, the comfort that isn't fake. Philosophy doesn't say the loss doesn't hurt. She reminds Boethius what Fortune never took: people who love him, his wife and sons still living, and his own mind, which no turn of the wheel can reach. And she adds something sharp: bad fortune can teach more than good. Good fortune flatters; bad fortune shows you your real friends. Fourth, a neighbor's version. The Stoic Epictetus said much the same in plainer words: never say of anything, I have lost it; say, I have given it back. Boethius gave the idea a picture people could hold: a turning wheel, and a voice explaining it.
screen: `YOU FORGOT WHAT FORTUNE IS.` · `FORTUNE SPEAKS: IT WAS ALL LENT.` · `WHAT THE WHEEL CAN'T REACH.` · `NOT LOST: GIVEN BACK.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL TURNS.`

segments.voice: Picture a slow wheel turning, and think of one recent turn of it in your life, up or down, something given or something taken. Then ask what the wheel didn't touch: who's still with you, and what's still yours inside. Rest there, at the hub, where the turning is slowest.
Fortune's wheel. In the Consolation, Fortune turns her wheel, lifting and dropping, and Philosophy says: you always knew she was like this. Today's word.
Your line: the wheel turns. The hub stays where it is. Day six hundred fifty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Boethius use the image of Fortune's wheel to meet gains and losses with less surprise, turning their attention to what no turn of fortune can take.

chat.says: Why did Philosophy tell Boethius he shouldn't be shocked that he lost everything?
options: Fortune always turns; he'd forgotten that all she gave him was only on loan.
His loss didn't really hurt, so there was no reason for him to grieve.
Fortune had made a rare mistake that she would soon put right again.
